message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This bid is unusual in that it is not based on assumptions about demand: we tested the exact opening pattern at Ashgrove before asking for a penny, and measured the results hour by hour. The pilot showed strong uptake, with evening visits running close to daytime levels and Sunday sessions very popular with families, and new memberships up by about two-thirds on the year before. That gives Members real local evidence that the hours will be used. The costing is equally careful. Staffing is built up from first principles, hours times staff times weeks times branches at the correct graded rate with on-costs, and utilities are taken from actual pilot spend rather than estimates, all of which sums to £174,000. We also looked seriously at the cheaper self-service alternative and explain why it would cost more once building works are included. I am confident this is a well-tested, carefully costed proposal that delivers on the Council Plan.
</author>

<document>
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.
</document>
response:
# Review: Extended Opening Hours Budget Justification

The case for extending hours has real merit, and Sunday opening in particular looks well supported by the pilot. But the costs don't add up to the total requested. The paper overstates evening demand, and it describes the pilot as twice its actual length. The value-for-money comparison also relies on Ashgrove, which the paper itself admits is the busiest branch. Corrected, the evidence supports Sunday opening strongly, but evening opening only weakly.

## Major issues

### 1. Table 2 sums to £164,000, not £174,000

The individual lines are correct:

| Item | Calculation | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Staffing | 10 × 2 × 50 × 5 = 5,000 hours × £24.80 | £124,000 ✓ |
| Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 × 5 branches | £32,500 ✓ |
| Kiosk maintenance | 5 branches | £7,500 |
| **Total** | | **£164,000** |

The paper requests **£174,000**, which is **£10,000 more** than its own costs. Either a cost line is missing, or the request should be reduced. Finance officers will notice this immediately.

### 2. Evening visits are well below daytime, not "close to" it

The paper concludes that evening visits "averaged close to the weekday daytime level." Table 1 shows:

| Slot | Visits per hour | As % of weekday daytime |
|---|---|---|
| Weekday 9 am–12 pm | 46 | — |
| Weekday 12 pm–5 pm | 58 | — |
| **Tuesday and Thursday 5–8 pm (new)** | **21** | **36–46%** |
| **Sunday 11 am–3 pm (new)** | **52** | **90–113%** |

Evening use ran at well under half the daytime level. **Sunday** is the strong result, and the paper should say so clearly. The evening results show modest demand, at the busiest branch in the borough. They do not show "strong latent demand."

### 3. The pilot lasted six months, not twelve

Section 3 says the pilot ran from October 2025 to March 2026, which is six months. The conclusion calls it "the twelve-month Ashgrove pilot." This matters for two reasons:

- **It overstates the evidence.** Six months of autumn and winter data can't show year-round demand. For example, summer evenings may be busier, or quieter.
- **The utilities costs come from the same six winter months.** Heating and lighting are higher in winter, so scaling those months up to a full year likely **overstates** the utilities cost. That is conservative, but worth stating.

### 4. The value-for-money figures use Ashgrove's rates for all five branches

The calculation of 84,000 visits is correct for Ashgrove's rates. Per branch, the new hours give (6 × 21) + (4 × 52) = 334 visits a week. Over 50 weeks and 5 branches, that's **83,500**.

But section 7 says Ashgrove is the **busiest branch** and that demand at the other four "may be lower." The value-for-money section then applies Ashgrove's rates to all of them anyway. If the other four branches see, say, half of Ashgrove's use, total extra visits fall to about **50,000**, and the cost per visit rises to about **£3.30**.

Two further problems:

- **Displaced visits.** Some Sunday and evening visitors would otherwise have come at another time. The real increase in library use is lower than the visit count.
- **Marginal against average cost.** The £3.40 borough average is a full cost per visit, covering buildings, book stock and overheads. The £2 figure is a marginal cost. They aren't like-for-like, so the comparison flatters the bid.

### 5. Evening hours cost much more per visit than Sunday hours

At the costs in the paper, each extended opening hour costs about **£65.60**:

| Component | Per hour |
|---|---|
| Two staff at £24.80 | £49.60 |
| Utilities (£6,500 ÷ 500 hours per branch) | £13.00 |
| Kiosk maintenance (£1,500 ÷ 500 hours) | £3.00 |
| **Total** | **£65.60** |

At Ashgrove's visit rates:

| Slot | Visits per hour | **Cost per visit** |
|---|---|---|
| Sunday | 52 | **~£1.26** |
| Evenings | 21 | **~£3.12** |

Even at the busiest branch, evenings cost about as much per visit as the borough average. At quieter branches they would cost more. This suggests offering Members options such as Sunday opening only, or Sunday plus one late evening, or phasing the evening hours in by branch.

## Moderate issues

6. **The self-service comparison is one-sided.** Self-service would save about two-thirds of the staffing cost, roughly **£83,000 a year**, against building work of **£300,000** (£60,000 × 5). The paper's own figures give a payback of about **3.6 years**, after which self-service is cheaper. That makes it more expensive only in the short term, which is not what the author's description implies. The building work would also be capital, not revenue. The job club and family activities are a valid reason to prefer staffed hours, and that argument should carry the case, rather than a cost comparison that doesn't hold over the life of the scheme.
7. **The memberships comparison isn't controlled.** 1,140 against 690 is a 65% rise, so "about two-thirds" is accurate. But it is compared with the previous year at Ashgrove only. Did memberships rise at the other branches, or across the borough, over the same period, for example because of a promotion or a library card campaign? Without that comparison, the rise can't be attributed entirely to the new hours.
8. **The staffing rate.** The Sunday working enhancement appears to be applied to all 5,000 hours, including the evening hours. If evenings don't attract an enhancement, the staffing cost may be slightly overstated. If they attract a different one, it should be shown.
9. **Kiosk maintenance.** It's not clear why a self-service maintenance contract is needed for staffed hours. A sentence of explanation would help.

## The author's description against the document

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| "Tested the exact opening pattern" | Correct, but over six months of winter only, and at the busiest branch. |
| "Evening visits running close to daytime levels" | **Incorrect.** 21 visits an hour against 46–58 in the daytime. |
| "Sunday sessions very popular" | **Correct.** This is the strongest result. |
| New memberships "up by about two-thirds" | Correct (+65%), but not compared with other branches. |
| Staffing and utilities "sum to £174,000" | **Incorrect.** The lines sum to £164,000. |
| Self-service "would cost more once building works are included" | Only for about the first 3.6 years. The paper's own figures show it's cheaper after that. |
| Document's "twelve-month pilot" | **Incorrect.** Six months. |

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the total to £164,000, or identify the missing £10,000 line.
2. Rewrite the evidence section to show Sunday as the strong result and evening use as modest.
3. Correct the length of the pilot to six months, and note the winter-only data.
4. Estimate demand at the other four branches, using their current daytime use relative to Ashgrove, and redo the value-for-money figures.
5. Compare marginal cost with marginal cost, or label the £3.40 average clearly as a full cost.
6. Offer Members options, such as Sundays only (about £66,000), Sundays plus one late evening, or the full package. Give the costs and expected use for each.
7. Present the self-service option over several years, and rest the case for staffing on the activities it makes possible.

A Sunday-only or phased proposal would probably have the strongest evidence behind it and the best value per visit. It would also give Members a clear choice rather than a single package built on overstated evening demand.
